Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 305 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
WMU 305 is located in the South Porcupine Hills, 
north of Pincher Creek. It is a large WMU that is 
bordered by Highways 3, 22, 2 and secondary road 
520. P
ortions of the unit lie within the montane,
foothills fescue and mixed-grass natural subregions of
Alberta. The Oldman River creates coulee habitat
along the southern portion of the WMU. Once amongst
the Porcupine Hills, rocky ridges and forest form a bulk
of the western half of the WMU while patchy Douglas
fir, poplar and shrub communities located within rough
fescue grassland shape the east. Coulee draws and
v
arying aspects along the eastern edge of the WMU,
where the hills convene with open grassland. WMU
305 was recently surveyed for Mule Deer in 2000 and
2010
 using the Random Stratified Block method and
r
ecently surveyed for a minimum total count of elk in
2007,2015 and 2020.
Survey Method 
A rotary wing (Astar-B3) transect survey was 
conducted February 13–17, 2025 flying 37 east-west 
lines at 1.85 km intervals, with 48 per cent coverage 
(800 m wide survey strip, area surveyed 1003 km2) for 
a total linear survey effort of 1254 km. At each 
observation point, ungulates were classified by 
species, and when possible, sex and age were 
recorded.  
Because transects varied in length, the average 
density (R) of mule deer, white-tailed deer, and moose 
(#/km2) was calculated by multiplying the number of 
animals per transect (Σx) by total area (km2) searched 
(total survey strip area [Σz]) (Jolly 1969, as described 
in Krebs 2014). Average density (R) was multiplied by 
the area (km2) of the WMU (Z) to determine population 
estimates with a 90 per cent confidence intervals. 
Confidence interval width was calculated by 
multiplying the t statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the 
Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error 
(SE; without replacement) of the abundance estimate 
where SE=sq root variance, and variance = N*(N-n)/ 
(n*(n-1))*(Σx2+R2*ΣZ2-2*R*Σxz) with N as the total 
number of possible transects given 100 per cent 
coverage, and n as the number of transects sampled.  
Moos
e and elk observations made during the survey 
were recorded even if outside of the transect width. 
Moose, mule deer and white-tailed deer data points 
were truncated to 800m strip width for population 
estimates. All elk observations were summed for a 
minimum total count.   
Results 
Mule Deer 
A total of 2291 mule deer were observed with an 
average group size of 12 (range 1-69). The estimated 
density was 2.70 mule deer/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 5717 individuals (90 per cent CI 4,955 
– 6,478). A total of 2084 mule deer were successfully
classified and the buck:doe:fawn ratio was estimated
t
o be 52:100:52. Due to the timing of the survey being
m
id-February, a small amount of antler drop had
oc
curred which will affect these ratios. The 2025
population estimate represents a 20% increase from
t
he last aerial ungulate survey population estimate for
mule deer within WMU 305 (conducted in 2010). The
s
urvey in 2025 also showed increases in both buck to
doe and fawn to doe ratios (Table 1). It is important to
not
e that the last survey used a different survey
methodology (Random Stratified Block).
White-tailed Deer 
A total of 361 white-tailed deer were observed with an 
average group size of 8 (range 1-33). The estimated 
density was 0.39 deer/km2 and the estimated 
abundance was 837 individuals (90 per cent CI 587-
1086). White-tailed deer were not classified into sex 
and age cohorts due to extensive antler drop having 
occurred by the time the survey was conducted. The 
2025 population estimate represents the only 
statistically rigorous method employed for white-tailed 
deer in WMU 305. 
Moose 
A total of 32 moose were observed on transect with 
and average group size of 1.1 (range 1-2). The 
estimated density was 0.037 moose/ km2 and the 
estimated abundance was 80 individuals (90 per cent 
CI 48 - 112). Moose have been generally counted 
anecdotally in past surveys for a minimum total count 
which likely greatly underestimated the previous 
population estimates.

El
k  
A total of 1014 elk were observed with an average 
group size of 46 (range 1-369). The bull:cow:calf ratio 
was found to be 16:100:24. The past surveys are 
presented in Table 1, however elk tend to migrate in 
and out of the WMU so no trends can be drawn. Also, 
this year’s survey was likely more intensive than in 
past surveys.
